text: Every column you've built so far describes one row. This lesson is about zooming out — splitting orders.csv into groups and summarizing each one, with real, hand-checkable totals by category and by region.

groupby category splits the 20 rows into their four category groups, then summing quantity and line_total adds those up within each group. You can check Footwear's $909.93 by hand — add up its five orders' line totals and you land exactly there.

Group by region instead, sum just line_total, and sort descending so the biggest region shows first instead of alphabetically. West leads with seven orders totaling eleven-eighty. All four regional totals add up to the full dataset — including the cancelled and negative-quantity rows, which is the catch coming up next.

Named aggregation lets you compute several different statistics in one call, each with a clear output name — order count, total quantity, total revenue, average order value — instead of chaining separate groupby calls for each one.

Here's the catch: none of those groupby calls excluded the cancelled order, the returned order, or the negative-quantity data error. Filter first, then group, and Footwear's total drops from $909.93 to $649.95 — a very different, more honest number.
You can now summarize this dataset every way that matters. Next lesson brings in a second table entirely — merging and joining DataFrames, pandas' answer to a SQL join.
